sections.title: Chairman's Chat - Farewell
sections.content:
Martin Baxter reports

All good things come to an end and, after 180 musings, this will be my final Chairman’s Chat.  I’m not sure who will be more relieved: me or you!  I have no idea how many members read Skywords but, since you are one of them, I hope that you will indulge me in a little reflection, having served on the committee for the past 19 years.

If I’m being honest there are times when it’s been a right pain in the backside: chairing and travelling to committee meetings and AGMs, hosting and making a speech at the Farmers’ Dinner, dealing with problems and complaints, answering questions, and writing articles.  

The COVID-19 lockdowns were a particularly challenging time, assessing all the differing views from Government, CAA, NHS, Police, BHPA, neighbouring clubs, MRTs, the media, landowners and the public, before asking members to respect our stance.    

I was in the chair on the only occasion when the club expelled a member.  I’ve also had to convince one member to give up the sport for his own safety, and for the benefit of his family.  I remain convinced that I probably saved his life.  Early in my tenure I spoke on behalf of the club at a member’s funeral.  

I also negotiated the Letter of Agreement with Leeds/Bradford Airport that allows us to fly at Baildon and Ilkley; and helped to defeat their proposed airspace ‘grab’ which would have limited our XC options and lost us at least one site.

It’s also been an immense privilege and honour to serve, working with a committee of like-minded members.  Like all of you I’m motivated by the thrill of flying, and sharing the experience with others, particularly through coaching.  I joined the committee after retiring from the Regular Army, feeling that I should give something back to the club that has done so much for me.  It’s certainly kept me occupied, whilst keeping the old grey matter ticking over..

Aside from the reasons given in my AGM report (below), as an ageing dinosaur, I’ve become increasingly frustrated by the smartphone trend towards Instant Messaging.  The club has an excellent website and a members’ only forum, but most of you appear to prefer an endless stream of messages where it’s difficult to sort the wheat from the chaff. Here today; gone tomorrow!  It’s often the case that short questions require lengthy answers; which probably already exist on the forum if members just took the time to look.  Our website also offers a comprehensive site guide, but I still see the occasional post asking for somebody to drop a pin.  Perhaps AI will come to the rescue.  Arghh!      

I hope to see you at the AGM where we’ll be electing my successor, and a committee to take the best club in the country into 2026 and beyond. I hope that you will do your best to support them. If you can’t make it, then I look forward to seeing you on the hill.

sections.title: AGM Report - Chairman
sections.content:
Martin Baxter reports

Committee

No mid-term casualties. Three committee members plan to step down at the AGM.

After 5 years Stef Sykes will be handing over as Social Secretary, although he will continue to help out with the annual FlyIn.

Having fulfilled the role of Competitions Officer over the last year Ed Cleasby has concluded that he can achieve what he wants to outside the committee, and that he can’t justify full committee participation. If nobody stands for the role at the AGM then it will be up to the new committee to decide how best to proceed.

After 16 years as Chairman, and 3 years as Sites Officer before that, I’ve decided that new blood is required. Hindsight is a wonderful thing: it’s only now that I realise that, having spent so long in post, I’ve allowed members to fall into the comfortable illusion that the club runs itself, and that your subscription is the only contribution required. That is totally unrealistic. The committee works hard on your behalf and it’s only fair that you do your bit by standing for a committee post at some stage.

We have established a new post on the committee – that of Airspace Officer.

Weather Station

Our Holfuy remote weather station was unserviceable from July – September due to a technical fault, which proved difficult to diagnose. Many thanks to Pete Logan and Liam Toothill for rectifying the problem.

sections.title: AGM Report - Safety
sections.content:
Clive Sury reports

All incidents reported to the BHPA by Dales Club members either in the UK or abroad should also be reported to the Dales Club Safety Officer, Rob Urselmann – safety@dhpc.org.uk. In this way any lessons learnt can be shared with our members.

There were 7 incidents reported either involving DHPC members or on DHPC sites in 2025. Two of these were at Nont Sarahs involving model aircraft. The Dales Club shares this site with the Pennine Soaring Club who take lead responsibility and are currently liaising with the modellers regarding clarity of airspace. Members are advised to be vigilant of model aircraft and observe the site airspace rules at this site.

Please be reminded that all reports help others learn and provide guidance on safety matters with the potential to reduce injury for all of us. Therefore, members are reminded and encouraged to report all incidents on the BHPA incident form here: Dealing with and reporting incidents and accidents. Plus, please send a copy of the report to Rob Urselmann for the club to benefit from any lessons learnt – email address: safety@dhpc.org.uk

If people would like to know the details of each incident reported on our sites within the last year, then these and all others reported can be found on the BHPA incident report log here: Incident Reports (Informal)

Of note is the use of the term ‘incident’ by the BHPA in lieu of ‘accident’. An incident is not just if someone is injured but also equipment failure or if an event could have resulted in an accident. The emphasis on regarding all these events as incidents is to encourage reporting of instances that could have led to more serious outcomes e.g., near misses, equipment failures or narrow escapes from injury. In this way, by reporting such ‘incidents’ wider learning can be made, and hopefully more adverse outcomes avoided in the future.

Therefore, re-iterating the point in the first paragraph, please submit incidents to both the Dales Safety Officer and BHPA when they occur. This helps yours and others safety knowledge. Thank you to everyone who has submitted a report, and I wish you all safe flying for the next year.

7 incidents

•        September – El Bosque, Algodonales Spain

•        August – Nont Sarahs

•        August – Dodd Fell

•        May – Taibridge

•        April – Windbank

•        April – Wether Fell

•        January – Nont Sarahs

New DHPC Safety Officer for 2026

From next year Rob Urselmann will be in the post as Safety Officer. I’d like to thank everyone in the Club for their help and support to me whilst I’ve held this role over the last 4 years, especially Martin Baxter as Chairman and fellow Committee members. I wish Rob every success in the role which I’m sure he’ll fulfil admirably in conjunction with the First Aid Training Days he’s organised for us to date.

2026 Reserve Re-pack Day booked for Saturday 17th January at Ilkley Grammar School.

sections.title: AGM Report - Chief Coach
sections.content:
Pete Logan reports

Coaching changes

We currently have 28 coaches for a club of 204, a very healthy number with a good geographic spread.

It was a bumper year for new coaches with Mike Barker, Jordan Whittaker, Pete and Rosie Darwood, Alan Oliver and Jake Herbert who were endorsed Club Coaches in spring. Thanks to Ed Cleasby and Steve Mann who refreshed their coaching endorsement this year as well.

New Pilot Ratings this year

Club members Chris Timson, James Maxwell, Jono Green, Marian Mansen, all gained pilot ratings this year. Congratulations to Simon Hulme, Stef Sykes and Mike Barker who also qualified as pilots this November too.

We have Pilot exams coming up in December and look to add a further three ratings.

Coaching Activity

The big event this year has been the BHPA clarification of what club pilots can and cannot do. TLDR; stay within sight or within reach of bottom landing. This prompted a good look at the club's existing club pilots and what their plans are regarding becoming pilot rated. I was able to communicate with half of our 80 CPs and get an idea of their intentions and make known how we can help them.

The 10 to 100km club which focuses on developing XC pilots has a number of graduates this year, Both Jordan Whittaker and James Maxwell knocking it out of the park in their first full year of XC. Elliot Brown too who shares membership at the Pennine Club.

We had informal coaching gatherings through the year, notably at the Fly In.

Next Year's Plans:

Continue the drive to increase the number of pilot ratings within the club.

sections.title: AGM Report - Sites (North)
sections.content:
Tom Shuttleworth reports

It’s been a steadily busy, but undramatic year for me as Sites Officer – which is probably where we want it to be.

Maintaining goodwill

A big part of our relationship-building efforts is the Christmas “booze run”. This sees a bottle and some shortbread or biscuits, delivered to all of our site contacts in December. At the time of writing, I’ve done about half of the 31 drop-offs for this year’s tour of the northern Dales. The primary purpose of the booze run is to express our appreciation and reinforce the goodwill that underpins our continued site access. In addition to allowing me to see people face-to-face, the gesture has consistently helped to maintain dialogue and trust over the years – which we really need if anything goes wrong. It costs about £750 plus mileage, so the club’s investment is not insignificant. But I think it goes a long way to help us avoid site fees and keep those good relationships.

Last year’s run also raised a couple of queries about the accuracy of our contact list. One lady admitted she wasn’t sure why she received an annual tin of shortbread (sadly for her, the confession means she won’t be receiving one this year..) Because of recent ownership changes, we are also seeing up to 4 people attending the Farmer’s Dinner, due to their control of access to one landing field we very rarely use. It’s not totally straightforward a) to understand exactly who the stakeholders are for any site – the overlay of ownership, farming/grazing/shooting/access rights are complicated and b) simply to cut people off if we don’t ‘need them’. So I’m trying to make sure our investment is heading to the right people, at the same time as avoiding the risk of causing unnecessary offence or bad will.

Site-Specific Issues

I had conversations with people about some potential problems at a few sites - with Nappa Scar, Tailbridge and Whernside being the most significant. These seem to have been mitigated, and issues/response were communicated at the time. As ever, reading and telling people to check the site guides remains the most important message. I have a number of other things to follow-up on relating to other sites, but none of these are about risks to our access.

Thanks

I’m grateful to many people who have helped me this year. Lots of you have let me know about things going on, suggested improvements, or conversations had – they are much appreciated. Martin’s gentle nudges for things I’ve forgotten, or should be considering, have been (genuinely) welcome, as have his direct intervention at times when I haven’t been able to. Special shout-outs also to Allan, Alan and Liam for bringing other things to my attention or dealing with things directly.

sections.title: AGM Report - PG Competitions
sections.content:
Ed Cleasby reports

I started out with ideas, good intentions and enthusiasm, but it turns out it's mostly just an admin job. This year there was plenty of it as records kept falling and the weather was pretty special in spells. I wanted to try 'task days' ... just simple, ridge based stuff to have a bit of fun, provide the opportunity for pilots to learn a little about flying a task and competing in a light hearted way. A bit like coaching plus. But, ideas are nought without people to help make it happen ...so it fell on stoney ground as no interest was expressed. The other thought was to follow this up with perhaps considering re entering/hosting the BCC with a team after a long absence. I don't think we are at this stage. The odd thing is, at one extreme we are near the top club in the UK, with a large group of really top pilots ... then nothing much coming through other than as individuals following their own Pilgrims Progress.

I was surprised at the amount of admin and this took me a while to get my head round as I dug deeper into all the updating that no one will probably ever see (except the mugs!). At least I now have that sussed... even if maybe too late. For seven years, outside the Comps title, I 've run the Northern Challenge Series, the X Dales for about five and done all the liaison for the BPcup (which we host). None of this requires me to have any Committee position, nor does doing the admin. So I've come to the conclusion that the position is supernumerary as far as I'm concerned and there really is no need for me to travel a long distance on winter nights at club expense. I'm still happy to do all the admin, run the various comps I've set up, liaise with the BPC, but in a more relaxed way, just outside the committee.

If anyone wishes to take it all on they are very welcome, but that would involve all I currently do ... not just a portion. I'll happily show them what's required.

sections.title: Wind Speed and Direction
sections.content:
Alan Oliver reports

Wind speed and direction – When out on a flight, be it local or an XC, the wind speed and direction is important, especially as we think about landing. Over the summer I have been doing a comparison of the calculated wind speed and direction between my FLYSKYHY and my XCTracer Max II. There has been some significant variation between the two.

You could pick any two devices and there would be significant differences. The reason for this is that the calculation for wind speed and direction is complicated and subject to assumptions. The instrument has no idea whether you are on or off bar, how the wind is gusting or how much brake is being applied. All it has to work from is your gps location, height and possibly G-force sensors. I know some devices like to see a 360 before showing wind speed and direction. However, both of mine seem to work before this.

On the other hand, Speed Over Ground (SOG) and Course Over Ground (COG) are trivial calculations and have been consistent between the two devices. My reason for writing this piece is that I have been caught out by thinking the wind speed was lower than it was, causing an unexpected cross-country trip. I have also got into the habit of checking SOG when coming in to land. By definition the lowest SOG is into wind.

To illustrate this I have created a graph (see below), that shows Speed Over Ground vs Course Over Ground for various wind speeds, for what I would consider to be a low B glider with a trim speed of 35kph. This leads me on to a number of theoretical observations that I have noticed, although not necessarily been able to quantify, on the hill. Remember, this graph is for Course Over Ground and not the direction the pilot is flying which is relative to the wind. The reason for plotting it in this way is that when ridge soaring, in an ideal world the ridge would be at 90 or 270 degrees to the wind.

subsections.title: Observations:o
subsections.content:
·        When heading downwind (0 or 360 degrees), speed over ground is trim speed plus wind speed.

·        When heading into the wind (180 degrees), speed over ground is trim speed less wind speed.

·        When ridge soaring (90 degrees or 270 degrees) with the wind square on the hill, speed over ground is always less than trim speed. This was a bit of a surprise to me as I had assumed it would be trim speed, but this does explain what I have experienced.

·        When ridge soaring with the wind 15 degrees off the ridge (shown by the two vertical lines) and a 30 kph wind speed, the difference from the downwind leg to the upwind leg is 28kph vs 12kph. So when slope landing, it is critical to get the upwind leg.

·        When ridge soaring with the wind 15 degrees off, but only 10kph, the numbers are 36kph vs 25kph . So when on the downwind leg, you are moving faster than trim speed. This is a typical speed where we might be slope landing due to lack of lift, so once again it is important to land on the upwind leg.

·        These last two points really emphasise that wind can be your friend.

·        When gale hanging, the difference heading into the wind which is 30 kph or 40 kph can be hard to spot. In both instances your speed over ground will be 5 kph, however you will either be going forwards or backwards. This can be hard to spot from height, so make sure you know how to read Course Over Ground from your instrument; better still, don’t get in this position in the first place.

·        When gale hanging (or going backwards) in a 40 kph wind, the best you can do is fly at 30 degrees downwind of the ridge (60 or 300 degrees on the chart).

Photo taken by Tom Shuttleworth

subsections.title: Conclusions
subsections.content:
·        I am in no way suggesting that you should be intentionally flying in 30 or 40kph winds, but in reality we all get caught out. My personal view is that I don’t normally take off in winds over 20kph and head for the landing field when SOG into wind is in low single digits.

·        Obviously all of the above calculations are on the basis of trim speed and you can always use the speed bar if needed.

·        If you need to use the speed bar then bear in mind the increased risks of a frontal collapse which could have serious consequences if near to the ground. So again I land when SOG into wind is in low single digits.

·        The ridges we soar in the Dales have all sorts of interesting features like bowls, Spurs, trees etc. When the wind is slightly off bear in mind what is in front of you on the upwind leg especially when coming into land as these features may create lee side turbulence. Semer water, Windbank and Whernside all suffer from this when the wind is off.

·         On a low B glider in particular, speed bar does not give a huge speed boost, so if you rely on it and the wind picks up further then the options are not good.

As we are coming into the winter season when the possibility of flying in stronger winds are more likely, I hope these observations prove helpful; writing this piece has certainly increased my understanding of the issues. Safe flying.

sections.title: Increase the Voltage!
sections.content:
Daedalus reports

Daedalus has always had a sneaking admiration for balloons, which achieve effortlessly what heavier than-air machines have to work so hard to maintain. The grave drawback of a balloon is that it needs a fresh supply of gas for every ascent, with all the expense, trouble, and danger that involves. Daedalus accordingly suggests a vacuum balloon, vacuum being even lighter than hydrogen. Unfortunately such a balloon would certainly collapse under atmospheric pressure.

Daedalus plans to balance this tendency by the self-repulsion obtained by giving the envelope an electric charge. He envisages in fact a combined balloon and van de Graaff electrostatic generator, with the balloon envelope serving as the storage capacitor. To preserve the charge-neutrality of the machine, two envelopes would in fact be needed, one to be charged positive, and the other to be charged negative; the van de Graaff machine would pump charge from one to the other. Both envelopes would expand under their stored charge, and would provide lift.

This elegant balloon would need no gas; its lift would be easily altered by varying the repulsion voltage (which would vary the equilibrium volume of the vacuum envelopes); it would in fact act as a silent and very economical vertical take-off machine. Daedalus's only worries are that it might tend to pick up waste paper when flying low, and it might be seriously affected by, or possibly cause, thunderstorms. (20 January 1966)

sections.title: Announcing the DHPC Reserve Repack Day
sections.content:
- Saturday 17th January 2026



When?  - SATURDAY 17th January 2026

– choose one of two sessions: 10:00am or 1:30pm

 Where? - Ilkley Grammar School, LS29 8TR.   GYMNASIUM – Springs Lane entrance.

 Who’s the repack for? - All pilots of all qualification levels and experience: hang gliders; paramotors; speedwings; paragliders.  Plus the event is open to both DHPC members and non-members

 Who’s doing it? - Guy Richardson, Ginger Nomad will be taking the lead with assistance from  other qualified re-packers

 Why should I do this?

A properly packed and fitted reserve can open within 30 - 50m of being thrown. Most manufacturers recommend repacking every six months (some as frequently as 90 days). There are several reasons for this:

Once the reserve is packed, it can absorb moisture from being left in damp air conditions, not just wet from rain. The moisture will not get back out again easily and can cause damage to the strength of fabric and lines as well as causing the fabric of the canopy to stick together.  

  • The reserve packed in the harness gets squashed. The effect of this is to almost iron creases into the reserve which have been shown to make the deployment slower, as the airstream takes longer to get between the leaves of the canopy to allow it to open.  
  • After about a year, the rubber bands that hold everything together long enough to deploy properly, can decay and need checking.  
  • Any Velcro in the system needs to be checked because if left for a long time it can get “welded” together, and it takes great strength to pull the reserve out. It has also happened that the Velcro on the side holders for the bridle on the harness did not open.  
  • A reserve can also be difficult or sometimes impossible to throw due to incorrect fitting to the harness
  • Finally - Can you refit your reserve if it accidentally falls out? It really is simple once you know how. If you cannot refit it safely then at best you could lose a day’s flying and at worst…

 What’s involved?

 Bring your reserve and harness and after a brief presentation from Guy, working in pairs with limited supervision and guidance from licensed BHPA re-packers on how to repack your reserve.

 Please note that this is event is for you to repack your own reserve under limited supervision and not a certified repack service.  Should you require this, you can arrange this with Guy Richardson directly who can collect/ deliver your reserve to you on the day, providing this certified service outside of the day itself.

 What do I need to bring with me?

  1. Your reserve and harness
  2. The printed reserve instructions for your make and model of reserve parachute.  It is best to have a printed version as reading on a phone has proved challenging in the past.  These should be available from the manufacturer’s website.
  3. A bit of string, paracord or something suitable for the packing loops on your reserve (if appropriate to your model) and also a bit of paraglider line or strimmer cord to assist with the pins when putting it in the harness.
  4. Suitable rubber bands to pack the lines. These should be available from Guy Richardson on the day.  However, the best option is to source the same rubber bands used by the manufacturer of your rescue chute - perhaps drop the manufacturer an email to see if they can point you in the right direction. Failing that, you could search the internet for size 8 rubber bands (not elastic bands). They should have as high a rubber content as possible - over 80% is good. One source is UK Airsports (note: I am not affiliated with UK Airsports).
  5.  Warm clothing - the venue may be cold.

 Are there any special offers on equipment on the day?

 Yes - Guy will offer discounts on reserves and other equipment. If you have a reserve that you think may need replacing, one option is to contact Guy in advance and he can bring it with him.  His contact details are:

 Ginger Nomad & Ginger Air

 What’s it cost?

 £25 - the money goes towards the hall hire, Guy and his assistants’ expenses, and Eventbrite’s booking fee.

 The event needs a minimum of 20 attendees to be financially viable.  Therefore, please book early if you plan to attend.

 

The Club is subsidising this event.  We will be reviewing attendance numbers and regrettably, if there are not 20 booked by January 5th 2026, then the event will not go ahead and refunds will be issued.

 How do I book a place?

https://dalesclubrepackday.eventbrite.co.uk

 Please keep to your morning or afternoon session.

 Anything else I need to know?

Yes,

1.     There are limited places for each session.  Therefore, it pays to book early to secure your place

 2.        Please ensure that you arrive on time for the session you book and leave after 2 ½ hours to allow either time for the next session or for us to clear the hall at the end of the day.  If you would like to ask me a question direct then please feel welcome to email me - safety@dhpc.org.uk

 3.        Finally, it’s good fun.  A great way to get to know others in the club, learn more about your equipment and be more confident about how the reserve functions.

Happy repacking,

Clive Sury.
